title: John the Baptist
english: A woman now dances and blinds the feast and stupefies the tyrant with the unlawful spectacle.
For she had a braid of hair ensnaring the young, a lining of eyes tripping up those who look.
She smeared rouge on her virtues, and the hook was not portable to those she met.
She opened her mouth, and belched death from her tongue.
She bent back her neck, and the sight was a procurer of corruption.
She bared her breasts, and provided a view of Hades' gates to curious onlookers.
She bared her thighs, hitching up the tunic of varied spectacle from her feet, and dragons hissing from her loins advanced toward corruption for the theater.
And the nod was deceitful, the glance filthy, the voice corrupting, the movement soul-destroying, the kiss death-bearing.
Yet Herod, caught, swore to give whatever the wicked dancing-girl might ask.
'And she, having been instructed by her mother: "Give me," she says, "here on a platter the head of John the Baptist."'
Do you see how great is the woman-mad pleasure.

Do you perceive how much corruption enslaves the one caught, how he who has been made soft by drunkenness no longer knows the scepter, does not remember his authority, lies exposed as a plaything to all.
For what did the dancing-girl utter to him?
'Give me here forthwith on a platter the head of John the Baptist.'

But these are not the words of one entreating, but of one commanding; for she does not approach the king as a maiden with fear or shame or any restraint, but as a mistress to a servant, as one having authority over bonds to a prisoner.
'Give me,' she says, 'on a platter the head of John the Baptist.'
Let him not delay the request.
Here I require the slaughter of the prophet, here to accomplish the murder of the one who reproves the adultery.
Where you beheld my nakedness, here I exact punishment from her triumphing dancer.
"Give me John's head on a platter."
Herodias commanded it; the adulteress gave the order.
If you refuse, you lose the one who commits adultery with you, and your bed will lie empty after the wine.
I withdrew from the couch — with whom should I now associate?
The mother shames the corruption; John sounds the trumpet, and she respects the servants but fears the guard.
Through John's boldness, the queen becomes a scandal to all.
Everyone treats her fate as a tragedy, but John is its cause — he has moved every tongue to speak before acting.
He sounded the trumpet against us first, unafraid to raise a pillar of shame for the queen by speaking of her adultery.
Moses lies asleep, yet through him comes a voice: the Law sleeps, but John awakens it against us.
He calls the queen an adulteress, and has persuaded many to follow him, to become bold.
translator_notes: The Greek text appears to be a continuous rhetorical passage, possibly from a homily or commentary on Mark 6, with OCR-induced line breaks but no missing letters at edges; no editor notes provided.
The phrase 'Ἰωάννου σαλπίζοντος' in [p5] is a genitive absolute construction, translated as 'John blowing the trumpet' for flow.
The metaphor of the Law sleeping and John awakening it draws on prophetic imagery of the Word stirring what is dormant.
All clauses from the source have been translated; no content omitted or invented.

title: Herod's Compromise
english: The king's vow to grant the girl's request was a reckless promise, for he was bound by his own oath and the presence of his guests.

Everyone knew that he was a slave to the adulteress and a captive of the dancer, as evidenced by the drinking party, the wine, the intoxication, the agreement of the oaths, and the king's unbridled promise.
He had sworn to grant whatever she asked of him, thinking that she would request something like bridal pearls, a field of ten thousand plants, or a city that he held as an exception in his kingdom.
However, she did not ask for anything that belonged to him, but instead sought the head of a prophet, which was something he was unable to provide.

The king wondered how he could possibly provide what she asked for, and noted that even if she had asked for heaven, he would not have been responsible for granting it, nor could he have given her the earth or the sea, for these things were beyond his authority and exceeded his power.
She said, 'Give me John the Baptist's head on a platter, for I thirst to drink his blood and gnaw on his limbs, and to see the head of the one who insults the kingdom with the royal dishes.'
She also stated that she must bring this dancing girl as a foreigner to her mother from the royal table, since Herodias awaits her share of the dinner from your own birthday.

If Herodias had demanded the tyrant's eyes, the king would not have become blind and sat on the throne, and similarly, if she had wanted to cut off his ear and nose, he would not have suddenly become a monster, and if she had ordered his hands to be cut off, the scepter would not have fallen from his fingers.
One might ask whether we should pity Herod's grief and ask the tyrant for forgiveness, for it was possible for him to dissuade the dancer and renounce the oath if he had wished to do so.
The natural law within him troubled him, and he was also afraid of the crowd and the multitude, for many people held the baptist in wonder.
Nevertheless, since he was eager for the murder and thirsty for the slaughter and considered the death of the prophet his own freedom, being persuaded by them…

translator_notes: The Greek text ends with the phrase 'δυσωπηθεὶς τοὺς', which is translated literally as 'being persuaded by them', but the sentence is incomplete.
The phrase 'ἀπὸ τῶν σῶν γενεσίων' is translated as 'from your own birthday' to reflect the genitive plural 'γενεσίων' (birthdays) and the possessive 'σῶν' (of you).
The verb 'ἐκδέχεται' in 'Ἡρῳδιὰς ἐκδέχεται' is rendered as 'awaits her share' based on context, implying expectation or reception of a portion.
The phrase 'ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης τῆς βασιλικῆς ξένιον' is translated as 'from the royal table as a foreigner' to reflect the ceremonial transfer of the dancer from the banquet setting.

title: The Triumph of the Word and the Role of Women
english: …He feigns oaths and, by the command of the girl, sends someone to serve the prisoner.

Thus, the head of the Baptist is brought upon a platter: the beauty of the prophets, the boldness of the word, the grace of repentance, the many-chambered pipe the God-sounding trumpet, the tongue that moves the clouds, eyes that behold the unsearchable things, ears that clearly hear the mysteries of God, a head that has touched the head of all.
And her, as it was given to the girl, a leopard bore the sacrifice of a lamb, while a wolf carried the head of a royal lion.
He brought the accuser to the mother, who did not cease his reproaches even after death, nor did he relinquish his boldness even after the slaughter.
But the prophet has fallen asleep, and the word is being handed down everywhere.
The trumpet has ceased, and the theaters of the inhabited world are filled with the sounds emanating from it.
The tongue has gone into the earth, and the sounds from it have filled the tribes.

He struck down the nations, thundering more strongly through every generation; for from that beginning, they spread through all the earth, proclaiming, 'Behold the Lamb of God, the one taking away the sin of the world' (John 1:29).
And you by no means from one woman of the whole world ran down nothing, because of a certain filthy vessel being now, but you cast down the whole ceramic of the maker.
For if even a woman closed the paradise, a woman again opened the royal step of the kingdom.
Women brought the flood by the race of the giants, but women opened the royal step by the dance of the apostles.
A woman tempted Joseph, but a woman nourished Elisha.
A woman bound Samson, but a woman commanded Barak; a woman sent Elijah into the wilderness in flight, but a woman hosted the same man while he was being tormented by famine.
A woman tripped Peter, and a woman became a protector of Paul, just as he himself is honored. Do you not seem to be weary of the word, wanting to sympathize with a woman?
But the one who is not weary will have the rewards brought to his feet briefly.

A woman labored with our redeemer. This one gave birth to and nursed the creator of the race, this one gave drink to the nourisher of the creation, the one who planned the springs for creation, in her arms she bore 'the one measuring the heavens with a span and the earth with a cubit,' the one who regulated and sealed the sea with his palm.
To him belong the glory and the power into the ages of the ages. Amen.
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence, and the subject of the first clause is missing.
The phrase 'the tongue into the earth' lacks a verb, though 'went' is implied by context.
The digit '8' at the end is an OCR artifact or page number and was skipped.
The text uses gendered examples to argue for the dignity of women in the service of the Word.
